messages.subject: Re: Ridge regression
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

think I slowly understand the whole concepts. In fact, it is very much what I described in another thread: http://www.r-inla.org/comments-1?place=topic%2Fr-inla-discussion-group%2F1G83cc6dRnA%2Fdiscussion

For any binomial or linear regression, alleles of single genes are used as covariates. If, however, a certain allele is not very frequent, the posterior distribution tends to have a too large variation. Or in other words: if allele A has a log OR of 1.3 +/- 0.5, allele B -1.3 +/-0.5, then the very rare allele C is unlikely to have a log OR of 0 +/- 100 ... only as an example. It is better and more to assume that log odds ratios are coming from a common Gaussian distribution.
In the thread  above, the undocumented model "z" is recommended. However: it seems to be better to use the concept described in the "stacks" example for ridging!

The mathematics in the model I thought about in this thread is in fact a little weird. The idea came, because I saw a tendency of the ridge regression to somehow "squeeze" the posterior distributions of ridged covariates to a zero-variance Gaussian distribution, if there is no relevant information in these covariates that explain the response variable. Inclusion of an "intercept" into the group of ridged covariates was therefore a very dirty approach.

The figure attached shows better what I think about the reality behind .... text boxes are (latent) variables, arrows show (the most important) feed-back and feed-forward influences, that might be modeled as functions of corresponding variables. My response variable is "MRNA Gene 1" expression levels, which is product of alleles A, B and C of gene 1. Specific activity for gene 1, i.e. transcription activation or inhibition for gene 1, is stimulated by gene 2 protein products. "Spontaneous source of activity" is the [partly structured] noise. Maybe it is not possible to express this whole model with R-INLA.Ideas?

If tried to do the modeling, to express mRNA as response variable in a linear regression, with gene 1 alleles as covariates, and gene 2 alleles as ridged covariates.
With MCMC, I would just model all influences and (latent) variables as a bunch of interconnected functions that finally calculate the response variable.

Best,
Andreas

and other coordinates, such as a lattice. In the lattice case, it can

inla.mesh.project/or merely provides a usually simpler alternative to
manually multiplying with a projection/mapping matrix as calculated by
inla.spde.make.A.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Variances in SPDE
messages.body_plain:
On 13/02/13 15:28, Karim Anaya wrote:
> A quick general question about  SPDE models  just to double-check Im
> not missing the point! are the variances of the finite-element
> representation of the Matern field the same (or just nearly the same)
> for all individuals/locations as it is usually assumed in traditional
> geostatistics?

At a distance of at least 1-2 times the correlation range away from the
boundary, yes, then they are approximately the same.  Closer to the
boundary the variances are inflated by a factor 2-4, typically
(depending on the domain geometry).  A more precise relation is given in
the 1D interval domain case in the Lindgren et al 2011 JRSSB SPDE/GMRF
paper, Appendix A I believe; For rectangular domains, a similar
expression holds, based on reflection in the domain edges.

The above of course only holds for the stationary SPDE operator case.
By letting the parameters depend on location one can for example
practically eliminate the boundary effect on the variance; this is
however not yet implemented in R-INLA.

Finn

>

> ## estimate 'a' and 'b'

>
> n = 1000
> x = rnorm(n)
> a = 1.1
> b = 2.2
>
> w = rpois(n,  lambda = exp(x))
> y = rpois(n,  lambda = exp(a + b*x))
>
> Y = c(w, y)
> X = c(1:n, rep(NA, n))
> XX = c(rep(NA, n), 1:n)

>     f(XX, copy="X", hyper = list(theta = list(fixed=FALSE)))
>
> r = inla(formula,
>         data = data.frame(Y, X, XX, A),
>         family = "poisson")
> summary(r)
>
>

On 18/02/13 11:31, Olga Lyashevska wrote:
> I am trying to understand how Delaunay traingulation works and I have
> here a few questions regarding my graph with 5257 vertices:

H Olga,

I'll answer briefly:

> 1. What defines here a boundary of the triangulation? Why are they so
> far extended? (I guess it relates to the recent discussion on
> variances at the boundaries?)

By default, the domain extended by a certain proportion around an
approximation of the convex hull.  In your case, it might make more
sense to specify a non-convex boundary instead, depending on what your
domain represents.

> 2. Are these triangles 'poorly shaped' (some of them are very elongated)?

Yes, the triangles in your figure are very "bad".  You appear to have
only asked for a triangulation of your existing points (plus the
automatic boundary), but you must also specify that you want a "refined"
triangulation; see more below.

> 3. Which algorithm is used for Delaunay triangulation?
> Why, for instance at the bottom of the convex hull I have only one
> point that seems to deform all triangles?

Since you did not ask for a refined triangulation, the program gave you
a pure Delaunay triangulation of your existing points.  If you instead
ask for a refined triangulation, points will be added iteratively at
strategic locations to improve the shape (and size) of the triangles.
See
   http://people.bath.ac.uk/fl353/isba/
for an example using inla.mesh.create.helper()

Finn L

For the benefit of the group/list, here's a quick summary of the solution to the problem.

Error in cbind(mesh$graph$tv[t.sub, c(1:3, 1), drop = FALSE], NA) :
>   subscript out of bounds
>

This error was a secondary error, due to trying to plot an empty mesh.
The mesh was empty because the shape data used to define the boundary was self-intersecting.
Since the triangulation software cannot deal with self-intersecting boundary edges (when a closed polygon is self-intersecting, "inside" and "outside"  is not well-defined), that left a gap in the boundary, leading the whole domain to be classified as "outside", and hence removed.

In this case the self-intersection was a very small loop, and could be ignored by setting the "cutoff" parameter in inla.mesh.create to a distance larger than the size of the loop.

As a side-effect of debugging this I've looked through the boundary handling code, and corrected some old annoying deficiencies.   The inla.sp2segment() function(s) will, from the next package update, support conversion from Polygon,Polygons,SpatialPolygons and SpatialPolygonsDataFrame.  inla.mesh.create.helper will handle boundaries without the user having to adjust 2D coordinates to 3D.

Finn

On Wed, 2013-02-27 at 10:26 -0800, Karim Anaya-Izquierdo wrote:
> I need just reasonable precision and Yes, it would be ok to use
> sampling! but how?

Hi

there is an experimental feature called

inla.posterior.sample()

see ?inla.posterior.sample, which can take a result object create by

r = inla(..., control.compute = list(config=TRUE))

and generate samples from the joint posterior, like

x = inla.posterior.sample(100, r)

due to the way the sampler is constructed, you may want to use some more
integration points, like using

r = inla(..., control.inla = list(int.strategy = "grid"),
control.compute = list(config=TRUE))

at least for not to many hyperparameters.

you have to extract the relevant components inside 'x', see str(x) and
str(x[[1]]), and from these samples, you can generate samples of the
variable of interest.

note that the posterior.sample() function is experimental, and future
changes may appear, and you'll get a warning about this when you run
it.

Best
